questions.body: What fundamental property defines a valid Binary Search Tree (BST)?
questions.keyPoints: For every node, all values in its left subtree are strictly less, and all values in its right subtree are strictly greater.

options.text: For every node, all keys in its left subtree are strictly less than the node's key, and all keys in its right subtree are strictly greater.
options.explanation: This property must hold recursively for all subtrees. An in-order traversal of a valid BST visits nodes in strictly ascending sorted order.

options.text: Every node must have exactly two child nodes.
options.explanation: That defines a full binary tree; BST nodes can have 0, 1, or 2 children.

options.text: The depth of left and right subtrees of any node never differs by more than 1.
options.explanation: That is the AVL tree balance factor property.

options.text: The parent node's value is always greater than or equal to both of its children.
options.explanation: That defines a Max-Heap property, not a BST.

questions.body: Which tree traversal order yields keys in ascending sorted order when applied to a valid Binary Search Tree?
questions.keyPoints: In-Order traversal (Left -> Node -> Right).

options.text: In-Order Traversal (Left, Root, Right)
options.explanation: Because a BST guarantees Left < Root < Right, visiting the left subtree first, then the root, then the right subtree produces values in ascending sorted sequence.

options.text: Pre-Order Traversal (Root, Left, Right)
options.explanation: Pre-order visits the root first, useful for tree cloning or serialization.

options.text: Post-Order Traversal (Left, Right, Root)
options.explanation: Post-order visits children before parents, useful for tree deletion or bottom-up evaluations.

options.text: Level-Order Traversal (BFS)
options.explanation: Level-order traverses by tree depth levels, not sorted order.

questions.body: How can you find the Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) of two nodes `p` and `q` in a Binary Search Tree in O(H) time and O(1) space?
questions.keyPoints: Start at root; if both p and q are smaller go left, if both are larger go right; the split point is the LCA.

options.text: Start at the root: if both `p` and `q` values are smaller than current node, traverse left; if both are larger, traverse right; the first node where they split (or match current) is the LCA.
options.explanation: The BST ordering property guarantees that the first node whose value falls between `min(p, q)` and `max(p, q)` is the lowest common ancestor where paths diverge.

options.text: Store the parent pointers of all nodes in a hash map.
options.explanation: While functional, storing parent pointers requires O(N) space, whereas BST walk takes O(1) space.

options.text: Perform a full Breadth-First Search level by level.
options.explanation: BFS does not take advantage of BST ordering and takes O(N) space.

options.text: Calculate the average depth of both nodes.
options.explanation: Depth alone does not identify ancestors.

questions.subtopic: Balanced Search Trees: AVL vs Red-Black
questions.body: Why are Red-Black trees preferred over AVL trees in many system libraries (such as C++ `std::map` or Java `TreeMap`)?
questions.keyPoints: Red-Black trees have looser balance rules, requiring fewer rotations on insertions and deletions (faster write performance).

options.text: Red-Black trees have slightly looser balance constraints, requiring fewer rotations during insertions and deletions, making write/update operations faster while maintaining O(log N) search.
options.explanation: AVL trees are more rigidly balanced (height difference at most 1), providing slightly faster lookup at the cost of more frequent rotations on updates. Red-Black trees strike a better balance for mixed insert/delete workloads.

options.text: Red-Black trees require 0 bits of extra storage per node.
options.explanation: Red-Black trees require 1 bit per node to store color (red/black).

options.text: AVL trees have O(N) worst-case search time.
options.explanation: Both AVL and Red-Black trees guarantee O(log N) worst-case search.

options.text: Red-Black trees can only store integers.
options.explanation: Both work on any comparable keys.

questions.body: What are the time and space characteristics of searching for a word of length `L` in a Trie containing `N` total words?
questions.keyPoints: Time complexity to search is O(L), independent of the total number of words N.

options.text: Search time is O(L) proportional only to the word length `L`, completely independent of the total number of words `N` in the dictionary.
options.explanation: Each character corresponds to one edge traversal in the Trie. Hence search, insert, and prefix lookup depend solely on word length `L`, making Tries ideal for autocomplete and IP routing.

options.text: Search time is O(log N).
options.explanation: Binary search over sorted arrays is O(L log N); Tries achieve O(L).

options.text: Search time is O(N * L).
options.explanation: Tries avoid comparing against all N words.

options.text: Tries require zero memory overhead for branching nodes.
options.explanation: Tries trade memory (storing pointer arrays or child maps) for fast prefix lookups.

questions.body: Which graph traversal algorithm is guaranteed to find the shortest path (minimum number of edges) between two vertices in an unweighted graph?
questions.keyPoints: Breadth-First Search (BFS) using a FIFO queue.

options.text: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
options.explanation: Because BFS explores vertices in increasing order of their distance (levels) from the source vertex using a FIFO queue, the first time the target node is visited is guaranteed to be via the shortest unweighted path.

options.text: Depth-First Search (DFS)
options.explanation: DFS explores deep branches first and can find suboptimal long paths.

options.text: In-Order Traversal
options.explanation: In-order traversal is specific to binary trees, not general graphs.

options.text: Topological Sort
options.explanation: Topological sort provides linear ordering of DAGs, not shortest paths.

questions.body: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's single-source shortest path algorithm using an adjacency list and a Min-Heap (Priority Queue)?
questions.keyPoints: O((V + E) log V)

options.text: O((V + E) log V)
options.explanation: Extracting each vertex from the min-heap takes O(V log V) total, and relaxing each edge and updating the priority queue takes O(E log V), yielding O((V + E) log V) total time.
O(V^3) is Floyd-Warshall for all-pairs shortest paths.

options.text: O(V * E)
options.explanation: O(V * E) is Bellman-Ford's complexity.

options.text: O(V + E)
options.explanation: Unweighted graphs with BFS run in O(V + E); weighted graphs require priority queue operations costing log V per step.

questions.body: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm fail when a graph contains edges with negative weights?
questions.keyPoints: Greedy choice assumption fails: visiting a node assumes its shortest distance is finalized, which negative edges can invalidate.

options.text: Dijkstra greedily assumes that once a node is marked visited/settled, its shortest path distance is finalized; a negative edge discovered later can yield a shorter path to an already visited node.
options.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy invariant relies on edge weights being non-negative so cumulative path distances only increase monotonically. Bellman-Ford must be used when negative edges are present.

options.text: The min-heap crashes when encountering negative numbers.
options.explanation: Min-heaps handle negative numbers properly; the issue is algorithmic logic.

options.text: Negative weights cause infinite loops in unweighted graphs.
options.explanation: Unweighted graphs do not have negative weights.

options.text: Dijkstra automatically converts negative weights to 0.
options.explanation: Simply converting or offsetting negative weights yields incorrect shortest paths.

questions.body: What unique capability does the Bellman-Ford algorithm offer over Dijkstra's algorithm?
questions.keyPoints: Handles negative edge weights and detects negative weight cycles in O(V * E) time.

options.text: It correctly computes shortest paths in graphs with negative edge weights and can detect the presence of negative weight cycles.
options.explanation: Bellman-Ford relaxes all E edges (V - 1) times. A V-th relaxation check that yields further distance reductions proves the existence of an reachable negative weight cycle.

options.text: It runs in O(V + E) linear time on dense graphs.
options.explanation: Bellman-Ford runs in O(V * E) time, which is slower than Dijkstra.

options.text: It can only be used on trees.
options.explanation: It works on general directed and undirected graphs.

options.text: It requires an adjacency matrix instead of edge lists.
options.explanation: It iterates directly over an edge list.

questions.body: Under what condition is a Topological Sort possible on a directed graph, and how does Kahn's algorithm find it?
questions.keyPoints: Graph must be a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph); Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes nodes with in-degree 0.

options.text: The graph must be a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG); Kahn's algorithm uses a queue to repeatedly process nodes with `in-degree == 0` and decrements neighbor in-degrees.
options.explanation: If a cycle exists, nodes in the cycle will never reach in-degree 0, so Kahn's algorithm finishes with fewer than V nodes processed, cleanly detecting cycle presence.

options.text: The graph must be undirected and connected.
options.explanation: Topological sorting requires directed edges (DAG).

options.text: Every node must have equal in-degree and out-degree.
options.explanation: That defines an Eulerian circuit condition, not a topological sort.

options.text: Kahn's algorithm requires a max-heap sorted by node values.
options.explanation: Kahn's uses a standard FIFO queue of zero-in-degree nodes.

questions.body: What is the nearly constant amortized time complexity per operation for Disjoint Set Union (DSU) using both Path Compression and Union by Rank?
questions.keyPoints: O(α(N)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function, effectively <= 4 for all practical values.

options.text: O(α(N)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function (effectively ≤ 4 for all universe-sized inputs).
options.explanation: Combining path compression (flattening tree during find) and union by rank/size yields an amortized bound of O(α(N)) per query, which is virtually O(1) in practice.

options.text: O(log N)
options.explanation: Union by rank alone without path compression is O(log N); combined they achieve O(α(N)).

options.text: O(N)
options.explanation: Naive DSU without optimizations can degrade to O(N), but optimized DSU is O(α(N)).

options.text: O(1) strictly worst-case.
options.explanation: The bound is amortized via the inverse Ackermann function, not strict worst-case per individual step.

questions.body: What is the core algorithmic difference between Kruskal's algorithm and Prim's algorithm for finding a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)?
questions.keyPoints: Kruskal sorts all edges and adds them greedily using DSU; Prim grows a single connected tree outward using a priority queue.

options.text: Kruskal's sorts all edges globally and adds them greedily if they don't form cycles (via DSU); Prim's grows a single tree outward from an arbitrary node using a priority queue.
options.explanation: Kruskal's algorithm is edge-centric (well-suited for sparse graphs: O(E log E)). Prim's algorithm is vertex-centric (well-suited for dense graphs: O(E log V) or O(V^2)).

options.text: Kruskal's only works on directed graphs.
options.explanation: MST is defined on connected undirected weighted graphs.

options.text: Prim's algorithm permits negative weight cycles while Kruskal's does not.
options.explanation: MST algorithms operate on undirected graphs regardless of edge sign (unless negative cycles create ambiguities in path formulations, but MST avoids cycles completely).

options.text: Kruskal's algorithm requires O(V^3) time.
options.explanation: Kruskal's runs in O(E log E) time due to edge sorting.

questions.body: When using DFS to detect a cycle in a directed graph, what edge classification confirms the presence of a cycle?
questions.keyPoints: Encountering a Back Edge (edge pointing to a node currently in the active recursion call stack).

options.text: Encountering a 'Back Edge' (an edge leading to an ancestor vertex currently active in the recursion call stack).
options.explanation: Using 3-color node states (White: unvisited, Gray: currently visiting in call stack, Black: finished), hitting a Gray node represents a Back Edge, confirming a cycle.

options.text: Encountering a 'Cross Edge' between two separate completed branches.
options.explanation: Cross edges in directed graphs connect vertices that are not ancestors of each other, which does not imply a cycle.

options.text: Encountering a leaf node with out-degree 0.
options.explanation: Leaf nodes terminate paths without cycles.

options.text: Visiting a vertex with in-degree greater than 2.
options.explanation: High in-degree merely indicates multiple incoming edges.

questions.body: How can a binary tree be uniquely serialized and deserialized using Pre-order traversal?
questions.keyPoints: By including explicit null markers (e.g. '#') for empty child pointers.

options.text: By recording explicit sentinel markers (e.g., `'#'` or `'null'`) for every null child pointer during pre-order traversal.
options.explanation: Standard pre-order alone is ambiguous. Including explicit null leaf markers ensures that reconstructing the tree via recursive pre-order reads unambiguously restores the original topology.

options.text: Pre-order alone is always sufficient without null markers.
options.explanation: Without null markers, multiple different tree shapes produce identical pre-order traversals.

options.text: By storing only the leaf nodes in order.
options.explanation: Leaf nodes alone discard internal parent structure.

options.text: By sorting all node values alphabetically.
options.explanation: Sorting destroys parent-child relationships.

questions.body: What is the diameter of a binary tree, and how is it computed in optimal O(N) time?
questions.keyPoints: Length of the longest path between any two nodes; computed via bottom-up post-order tracking max(left_height + right_height).

options.text: The length of the longest path between any two nodes in the tree; computed in O(N) using post-order DFS where each node returns its height and updates `max_diameter = max(max_diameter, left_h + right_h)`.
options.explanation: The longest path may or may not pass through the root. Bottom-up post-order calculates subtree heights and evaluates the path passing through each node as a candidate diameter in a single pass.

options.text: The total number of leaf nodes in the tree.
options.explanation: Diameter is a path length (number of edges or nodes), not leaf count.

options.text: The height of the root node multiplied by 2.
options.explanation: The longest path does not necessarily pass through the root.

options.text: Computed by running all-pairs shortest paths in O(N^3).
options.explanation: Tree topology allows linear O(N) calculation via simple DFS.

questions.body: What graph condition is equivalent to a graph being Bipartite (2-colorable), and how is it verified?
questions.keyPoints: A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd-length cycles; verified using 2-color BFS/DFS.

options.text: A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains NO odd-length cycles; verified in O(V + E) by attempting to 2-color the graph using BFS or DFS.
options.explanation: If during BFS/DFS traversal an adjacent neighbor already has the same color as the current node, an odd cycle is detected, proving the graph cannot be partitioned into two independent sets.

options.text: The graph must be a complete graph K_n.
options.explanation: Complete graphs with > 2 vertices contain triangles (odd cycles) and are not bipartite.

options.text: Every node must have an even degree.
options.explanation: Even degrees is the Eulerian condition, not bipartiteness.

options.text: The graph must have no edges.
options.explanation: Bipartite graphs can have many edges (e.g. trees are always bipartite).

questions.body: What is a Strongly Connected Component (SCC) in a directed graph?
questions.keyPoints: A maximal subgraph where every vertex is reachable from every other vertex in the subgraph.

options.text: A maximal subgraph where every vertex is reachable from every other vertex in the subgraph.
options.explanation: In an SCC, directed paths exist between all pairs of vertices within that component. Tarjan's algorithm and Kosaraju's algorithm both find all SCCs in optimal O(V + E) time.

options.text: A subgraph with no directed cycles.
options.explanation: An SCC with > 1 vertex fundamentally requires directed cycles to achieve mutual reachability.

options.text: A tree spanning all vertices with minimal edge weight.
options.explanation: That is a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST).

options.text: A clique where all pairs have bidirectional edges.
options.explanation: SCC paths can be multi-hop indirect paths, not necessarily direct single-edge cliques.

questions.body: What bitwise trick allows a Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree) to isolate the Lowest Set Bit (LSB) of an integer `x` for index navigation?

options.explanation: Due to two's complement representation, `-x = ~x + 1`. Performing `x & (-x)` zeroes out all bits except the lowest set bit, enabling O(log N) prefix sum updates and queries.
`x ^ (x - 1)` flips all trailing bits including the lowest set bit.
`x | (~x)` evaluates to all 1s (-1).
Right-shifting shifts all bits by one position.

questions.body: What capability does a Segment Tree possess that a standard Fenwick Tree cannot easily support?
questions.keyPoints: Arbitrary range queries (such as Range Minimum/Maximum Query, RMQ) and Lazy Propagation for range updates.

options.text: General non-invertible range queries (such as Range Minimum Query, RMQ) and Lazy Propagation for O(log N) range updates.
options.explanation: Fenwick trees rely on invertible operations (`sum(L, R) = prefix(R) - prefix(L-1)`). Operations like `min` or `max` are non-invertible. Segment trees store intervals explicitly, handling arbitrary associative operations.

options.text: Segment trees take O(1) space while Fenwick trees take O(N^2).
options.explanation: Fenwick tree takes O(N) space; Segment tree takes O(4N) space.

options.text: Segment trees cannot be updated after construction.
options.explanation: Segment trees support point and range updates in O(log N).

options.text: Segment trees only work with integer values.
options.explanation: Segment trees operate on any algebraic monoid/semigroup.

questions.body: What algorithmic concept ensures termination and optimal O(V * E^2) time complexity in the Edmonds-Karp implementation of the Ford-Fulkerson maximum flow method?
questions.keyPoints: Using Breadth-First Search (BFS) to find the shortest augmenting path (in terms of edge count) in the residual graph.

options.text: Using Breadth-First Search (BFS) to consistently select the shortest augmenting path (fewest edges) in the residual graph.
options.explanation: Standard Ford-Fulkerson with DFS can choose paths that result in exponential iterations or non-termination with irrational capacities. Edmonds-Karp uses BFS, guaranteeing monotonic increase in shortest path distances in O(V * E^2).

options.text: Sorting all edges by flow capacity in descending order.
options.explanation: That is capacity scaling, a different variation.

options.text: Using Dijkstra's algorithm with negative edge weights.
options.explanation: Edmonds-Karp uses BFS on unweighted edge counts.

options.text: Eliminating all back edges in the residual graph.
options.explanation: Residual back edges are mandatory to allow flow cancellations/redirections.
